quote: I can tell people. You gotta be stupid to take from me.
stewart_read: This pre-intro fragment (likely mid-conversation with someone else before the call connects, or a defensive aside) suggests the customer has a guarded, transaction-skeptical posture before the rep even speaks. It sets up his fast pivot to 'can this be done via email' as consistent with someone who doesn't want to be worked.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be unrelated background noise/crosstalk with no bearing on the customer's actual disposition toward the rep.
coaching_implication: Not directly actionable, but worth noting as color for why this customer resisted the standard funnel — he opened already defensive, not neutral.

quote: I don't need all the other stuff. I'll look at it. If it looks good and everything is good to go, then, obviously, I'll choose you guys to get services with.
stewart_read: The customer is essentially pre-committing to buy if the numbers work — this is close to a self-generated 'what's expensive is not switching' opening, and the rep never uses the customer's own conditional commitment as leverage to get him on a call instead of email.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that pushing harder here would lose the customer faster; staying neutral could be a deliberate de-escalation, not a missed flip.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to mirror the customer's own words back — 'so if the numbers work you're in — that's exactly why our specialist walks the numbers live with you' — turning the customer's conditional buy-in into a reason for the call, not a reason to skip it.

quote: Yeah. No. I mean and that's what everybody says. You know what I mean? Like, I I I've been in sales, and I and I used to sell for solar too.
stewart_read: The customer discloses direct competitive/industry background (worked in solar sales himself) and that he's already talked to multiple solar companies — this is exactly the kind of prior-contact disclosure the verify section's prior_designs item is built to capture, and the rep does not probe which companies or what he was shown.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that probing here would read as stalling to an impatient customer who already said he wants to end the call quickly.
coaching_implication: A 10-second question — 'oh yeah, who'd you sell for, and what are the other quotes you've gotten showing?' — costs little with an impatient customer and gives the closer real competitive intel; flag this as a skipped low-cost probe.

quote: So that's why I said I I just if I can just email you the p and m Mhmm. So you can go ahead and review it.
stewart_read: The customer hands the rep his own PNM bill and satellite-imagery point as an anchor — a direct hook the rep could reflect back ('once we pull that, our specialist can show you the actual number live') to make phone conversation more attractive than email. Instead the rep files it and continues repeating the appointment-format ask.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep did attempt a related move one line later at 03:12 ('we can get this done in, like, two seconds, get that bill real quick') — but this reused the same channel-format argument rather than building curiosity around what the bill would reveal.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to turn an offered document into a curiosity hook ('once we see that, we'll know exactly what you'd offset — the specialist can show you that live in five minutes') rather than only re-litigating in-person vs. phone vs. email.

quote: Electricity panel to see if you guys need to add anything, to be able to add the solar panels on to my home.
stewart_read: The customer raises whether his electrical panel needs an upgrade to support solar — a real technical/scope question not covered in the current schema's cross-sell catalog (which only documents roofing). This isn't a roofing signal, but it is a service-scope question the rep doesn't address or route.
alternative_hypothesis: This may not be a revenue-relevant cross-sell at all if Ion doesn't sell electrical panel upgrades — in which case it's simply a technical question the rep correctly should defer to the specialist.
coaching_implication: Flag for Kenny: does Ion's cross-sell catalog include electrical panel upgrades? If yes, this is an uncaptured signal; if no, the rep's silence here is scope-appropriate and no coaching action is needed.

quote: We'll get what is your warranty on the panels and, that stuff.
stewart_read: The customer asks a closer-tier product question (warranty terms) and the rep never answers it directly, but also never deploys the clean escape hatch language ('that's exactly what the specialist walks you through') — he lets it sit inside the broader channel argument instead of explicitly bridging it.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's later line 'I'll literally tell them you just wanna be straight up straight to the point' implicitly defers the warranty question to the phone-call specialist, so this may already be handled adequately rather than missed.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to explicitly name-check unanswered questions when bridging — 'warranty, pricing, panel count — that's exactly what they'll cover on that quick call' — so the customer hears his specific questions acknowledged, not just a generic reassurance.

quote: what if I cut the in person appointment and I all that sit down stuff? If I remove that and I set you up with just a phone call and all they do is they call you, they Gmail you, and then you guys just go over it together.
stewart_read: The rep offers to have the specialist 'Gmail' the customer as part of the phone-call setup — this brushes right up against the hard rule of not sending proposals before the meeting; it's an improvised soft concession under pressure, not a scripted response.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may just mean the specialist will email logistics/confirmation, not the actual proposal — the line is ambiguous enough that this could be an innocuous scheduling detail rather than a policy compromise.
coaching_implication: Clarify with the rep what 'Gmail you' meant in the moment — if it implied sending numbers before a live walkthrough, that's a hard-rule risk worth correcting explicitly.
